title: Delhi AQI at 321 as Severe Pockets Persist and GRAP Stage III Stays in Force
excerpt: The capital's CPCB average was 'very poor' at 7 a.m. on November 12, with IIT Delhi at 408 in the severe band; international dashboards showing 'hazardous' use a different US scale.
body:
• Delhi's overall air quality index stood at 321 in the "very poor" category at 7 a.m. on Thursday, November 12, according to Central Pollution Control Board data reported by ANI.
  • Some monitoring stations were far worse: IIT Delhi recorded 408, in the "severe" band, in station readings reported around 5 a.m., while NSIT Dwarka, Chandni Chowk and Pusa all stood near or above 380.
  • GRAP Stage III restrictions remain in force across Delhi-NCR; the full list of what is banned and allowed is in the GRAP Stage III explainer.
  • Readings shown as "hazardous" above 500 on some international dashboards use the US AQI scale, a different scale from India's CPCB index — the two numbers are not directly comparable.

Delhi woke to another morning of smog on Thursday, November 12, with the city's overall air quality index at 321 in the "very poor" category at 7 a.m., according to Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) data reported by ANI. PM2.5 and PM10 remained the major pollutants across the capital.

The citywide average concealed much worse pockets. In station readings reported around 5 a.m., IIT Delhi recorded an AQI of 408 — inside the "severe" band — while ITO stood at 391, North Campus at 390, Chandni Chowk at 389, DTU at 384 and Pusa at 379, according to the CPCB station table published by Jagran Josh. ANI's 7 a.m. round put NSUT Jaffarpur highest at 399, followed by Chandni Chowk at 387 and Pusa (IITM) at 386.

Two scales, two alarming numbers

Some live dashboards showed Delhi in a "hazardous" band above 500 on Thursday morning. Those dashboards use the US Environmental Protection Agency's AQI scale, which runs higher than India's CPCB scale for the same air. India's scale classes 0-50 as good, 101-200 as moderate, 201-300 as poor, 301-400 as very poor and 401-500 as severe. Both scales agreed on the underlying point on Thursday: the air was unhealthy across the capital, and worst in the early morning hours.

GRAP Stage III stays in force

The Commission for Air Quality Management has kept GRAP Stage III restrictions in force across Delhi and the adjoining districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, as pollution has failed to settle since Diwali on November 8, when several stations crossed into the severe category and visibility dropped in the early hours. What is restricted under Stage III — and what remains allowed — is set out in the stage-by-stage GRAP explainer.

What this means if you are travelling or have family in Delhi

For diaspora readers with family in Delhi-NCR — and for anyone flying in this week — the practical exposure is the morning hours, when readings peak. Neighbouring NCR cities were also elevated on Thursday morning: Noida's Sector 62 recorded 379 and Gurugram's NISE Gwal Pahari 359 in the same early readings. Mumbai, by comparison, recorded 146 in the moderate category on CPCB data. Outdoor exercise in the early morning is the exposure health advisories consistently target first at these levels; masks rated for fine particles and indoor air purification are the standard household mitigations while Stage III remains in force.
